chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
title: Earl Hines's singers and a loose band vs Lunceford's discipline
summary: Hines had singers Herb Jeffries and Arthur Lee Simkins, and Young did not want to leave a free band for strict Lunceford.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: After I left. When I was with Earl Hines we had two singers. The first one was Herb Jeffries. And the next singer was a Georgia boy, Arthur Lee Simkins.

He came in. And then the girl singer was Ida James: Ida was with Earl. There was another girl singer. I can't -- Madeline Green. I don't know if you remember her. She was with him too. But Budd Johnson was on that band. Ray Nance was on. In fact, Ray Nance was the guy who encouraged me to go with Lunceford. I wasn't going to go because I was having too much fun with Earl.

Earl's band was loose, you know, like no restrictions but Lunceford was -- you know, like you have to do this exactly like that. And, you know, when you're young you don't like -- you don't go for that too much, you know. And everything was just -- had to be just so and so.

It wasn't like that with Earl. We were loose, you know. You just did what you want to, man. You know, you just played. But with Lunceford, I knew I couldn't take the chances and experiment as much as I did with Earl. So, I didn't experiment a whole lot when I went with Lunceford because I had done all that with Earl. But I was going to experiment more if I had stayed with Earl. No telling what I wouldn't have wound up doing, you know.
